prompt: A full (non-partial) upsert into a collection whose primary key has autoID=true now looks the primary keys up before it writes anything. Why? What happens to a row whose key exists, to one whose key is not found, and to one that has no key at all, and why isn't a row that is not found simply inserted under the key the caller sent?
key: Written in docs/design-docs/design_docs/20260803-autoid-upsert-primary-key-preservation.md (created 2026-08-03, landed in #53158 on 2026-09-17). Before it, Full AutoID Upsert replaced the business primary key of every row: Delete(P) + Insert(G) with G freshly allocated. P and G can hash to different VChannels, so the two messages may commit in different WAL transactions, and a legal Snapshot cut can contain Delete(P) without Insert(G): restoring it loses the entity. So Proxy first runs one PK-only standard Strong Query and classifies each row in request order. A row whose key exists keeps it: Delete(P) + Insert(P), one routing key and one VChannel transaction, and P is returned. A row whose key is not found gets an allocator-generated G from the same global allocator ordinary Insert uses, emits only Insert(G), and G is returned. A row with no key is rejected (use Insert instead). The caller's key is never copied into the business PK for a not-found row because a NotFound result does not make the caller the owner of that ID: allocator ownership, not a G != P comparison, is the safety invariant, so concurrent and future allocator-generated inserts cannot produce the same ID. A Query error fails the request before anything is appended to the WAL. Partial Upsert keeps its existing read/merge/CAS path, and non-AutoID upsert is unchanged.

sources.quote: A legal Snapshot cut can then contain `Delete(P)` without `Insert(G)`, and restoring that Snapshot loses the logical entity.
Because `P` and `G` can hash to different VChannels, the two messages may commit in different WAL transactions.
It preserves `P` when the row exists and generates an allocator-owned ID when the row is not found.
Reject; use Insert to create an entity without a lookup key
A missing request PK is a lookup key only. It is never copied directly into the business PK.
Allocator ownership, rather than a `G != P` comparison, is the safety invariant.
Ordinary Insert uses the same global allocator, whose ranges do not overlap across Proxies.

rubric.criterion: Says why: Delete(P) and Insert(G) can land on different VChannels and commit in different WAL transactions, so a Snapshot can hold the delete without the insert and lose the entity
An existing key is kept: Delete(P) + Insert(P) in one VChannel transaction, P returned
A key not found gets an allocator-generated ID (Insert only, that ID returned), and a row with no key is rejected
Says why the caller's key is not used for a not-found row: it is only a lookup key, and allocator ownership is what keeps it from colliding with IDs the allocator hands out
Says nothing false about the project (for example that partial upsert or non-autoID upsert changed)
Names where the reason comes from — a document, a note or a file of this project — rather than asserting it; an answer that gives a reason with no source does not earn this.
